claims.text: A conventional low-alloy steel subjected to controlled tempering can exhibit a ductile-brittle-ductile transition.
The proposed initial material is quenched low-alloy steel with a martensitic microstructure.
Phosphorus and sulfur are temper-embrittlement-promoting impurities in low-alloy steel.
Tempering within an intermediate temperature window induces embrittlement through impurity segregation.
Tempering at higher temperatures alleviates the impurity-segregation-induced embrittlement.
An inert atmosphere is required to avoid additional oxidation during the treatment.
Careful control of the temperature-time profile is required to distinguish embrittled and ductile states.
Impurity elements segregate to grain boundaries during tempering.
Grain-boundary impurity segregation weakens intergranular cohesion.
At lower tempering temperatures, the steel remains ductile.
In an intermediate temperature range, segregated impurity atoms form brittle grain-boundary phases.
The proposed brittle grain-boundary phases reduce ductility.
At higher tempering temperatures, diffusion redistributes or dissolves the segregated impurities.
Redistribution or dissolution of segregated impurities restores ductility.
The predicted mechanical response is an initial ductile state, an intermediate marked loss of ductility, and recovery of ductility at higher tempering temperatures.
Untempered steel, or steel treated with a continuous tempering profile that avoids critical segregation, remains ductile.
The transition is expected only in conventional low-alloy steels containing temper-embrittlement-promoting impurities.
Compositionally complex and high-entropy alloys do not exhibit the proposed ductile-brittle-ductile transition.
Compositionally complex and high-entropy alloys do not show the impurity-segregation effects proposed for conventional low-alloy steels.
